## Learning goals

- I will be able to design a table for repeated measurements.
- I will be able to write measurements to CSV with Python.
- I will be able to validate, preserve, and document raw data.

This is important because it enables me to turn observations from electrical and computer systems into evidence that can be checked and analyzed.

## Progression

1. Begin with a small teacher-provided dataset such as time, voltage, current, and temperature.
2. Identify the independent variable, dependent variables, units, expected ranges, and missing-value rule.
3. Write a Python program that appends one complete row to a CSV file.
4. Add a timestamp and a clear header row.
5. Reject values outside the teacher-approved range instead of silently saving them.
6. Open the CSV in a text editor and spreadsheet to confirm that the structure is portable.
7. Commit the program and a small non-private sample dataset.

Keep raw data unchanged. If you clean or transform it, save the result as a new file and document what changed.

## Evidence

Submit the Python file, sample CSV, terminal output from a successful run, and a data dictionary explaining each column and unit.

## Extend your learning

- Read Python's official [`csv` module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html).
- Add command-line arguments for the output filename.
- Record a sensor simulation at a fixed interval without connecting physical hardware yet.

## Review and reflect

Why are units and column names part of the data? Why should raw measurements be preserved before analysis?
